title: Data Products
text:
Three data releases on Zenodo accompany my papers on the middle class in Africa. The cell-level data rest on incomes from the Gallup World Poll, and the economic-class shares rest on consumption imputed into Afrobarometer. The two welfare measures differ, and each set of shares stands on its own.


Mapping Africa’s Middle Class Across Space: cell-level data
with Tobias Heidland
Version 1.0 (November 2026), CC BY 4.0
Data (Zenodo) · Paper (SSRN)
Predicted middle-class shares for 159,698 populated cells of 96 km² in 55 African countries, under six income definitions, 2015–2023, with sums by country, province and district. The method is described in Mapping Africa’s Middle Class Across Space.




Economic Class of Afrobarometer Respondents: Imputed Consumption under Five Middle-Class Definitions, Rounds 3–9
Version 1.0 (November 2026), CC BY 4.0
Data (Zenodo) · Paper (SSRN)
The class shares of every country and country-round under five published middle-class definitions, with each component of their standard errors. The household series covers 302,595 respondents in 42 countries and 215 country-rounds of Rounds 3 to 9, and the adult series covers 100,113 respondents in 39 countries and 73 country-rounds of Rounds 8 and 9. The shares come from consumption imputed into Afrobarometer with a model estimated on 49 household-expenditure surveys in 25 countries. The respondent-level files are available on request under Afrobarometer’s terms. The method is described in Estimating Economic Class in Afrobarometer Using Survey-to-Survey Imputation.




Harmonized Afrobarometer Variables: Cross-Round Mapping and Comparability Codes, Rounds 1–9
Version 1.0 (November 2026), code under the MIT license, mapping and documentation under CC BY 4.0
Mapping and code (Zenodo) · Paper (SSRN)
Afrobarometer’s round files name and code the same question differently across rounds. The record maps the 1,897 round variables that recur in at least two of Rounds 1 to 9 onto 386 common variables, with each round’s question text. It also codes the comparability of the consumption model’s predictors by round and holds the code that rebuilds the harmonized file. The code runs on the round files that users download from Afrobarometer.

Sékou Metiki

  FieldsDevelopment Economics · Political Economy · Machine Learning
  MethodsSurvey-to-survey imputation · Machine-learning ensembles · Shift-share designs · Geospatial data
  ToolsR · Python · Stata · QGIS · LaTeX
  LanguagesFrench (native) · English (fluent) · German (intermediate)

I am a PhD researcher at the Kiel Institute for the World Economy and submitted my dissertation at Kiel University (CAU) in November 2026.

Job market paper
Where the Windfall Lands: Export Booms and the Demand for Democracy in Africa

Do economic windfalls strengthen popular demand for democracy? Modernization theory predicts that higher household incomes increase demand for democracy by reducing reliance on political patrons, while rentier theories predict that windfalls captured by the state reinforce patronage and dependence. I link 125,659 Afrobarometer respondents (2005–2022) in 2,198 districts of 22 African countries to baseline crop maps and world prices. In a shift-share design that controls for expected price exposure, I compare districts with higher and lower shares of residents employed in farming. I find that demand for democracy rises more in districts where more residents farm when world prices of their export crops rise. For a one-standard-deviation three-year boom, the response is 0.025 standard deviations higher in a district with a 25-percentage-point higher farming share (p = 0.061 under a randomization test over the six price series). This is consistent with windfalls supporting democracy where they reach households and equally with state patronage lowering demand where few residents farm.

Paper (SSRN)

My research produces reliable data on Africa where such data are scarce, particularly on poverty, inequality and the size of the middle class. I combine household surveys, satellite imagery, infrastructure data and machine learning to estimate consumption and middle-class shares across African countries under competing definitions. I also worked in the DYNAMIG project, which collected primary data through a multi-country online survey on living conditions and migration attitudes in Africa.
Building on these measures, I study the political economy of development. In my job market paper, I examine how export booms relate to the demand for democracy across African districts, linking crop maps and world prices to Afrobarometer respondents.
I also work on international macroeconomics. I study how central banks prepare for foreign exchange intervention through their exchange rate regime, the level of their reserves and the share of reserves available for intervention. The paper, written with Tobias Heidland and Lukas Menkhoff, has been revised and resubmitted to the Journal of Money, Credit and Banking.
The data of the two papers on the middle class are public on Zenodo in three releases.

title: Research
text: My research asks who benefits from export booms in African economies: how much of a rise in world crop prices reaches farming households, how much the state retains, and how citizens’ demand for democracy responds. I also develop methods to measure household living standards where expenditure and administrative data are limited.

title: Research
text:
Under Review



Preparing for FX Intervention
with Tobias Heidland and Lukas Menkhoff
Journal of Money, Credit and Banking, Revised and Resubmitted (Last updated November 2026)
Paper (SSRN)

Most central banks do not publish their foreign exchange interventions (FXI), but the preparations that enable their interventions are visible. We measure FXI preparedness through three policy decisions, namely the rigidity of the exchange rate regime, the level of official reserves relative to GDP and the share of reserves held in assets available for intervention. For the last of these, we build a new index from the IMF’s data on reserve composition. Better-prepared countries intervene more, so preparedness indicates a willingness to intervene where intervention data are not published. Between 2001 and 2020, preparedness rose with more rigid regimes and larger reserves, while aggregate intervention did not keep pace. Preparedness is higher in economies with lower income, greater trade openness and more volatile portfolio inflows.

title: Research
text:
Working Papers



Estimating Economic Class in Afrobarometer Using Survey-to-Survey Imputation
Working paper (Last updated November 2026)
Paper (SSRN) · Data (Zenodo) · Variable mapping and code (Zenodo)

Afrobarometer, the principal pan-African attitude survey, omits consumption and income. As a result, the economic class of its respondents is unknown. I impute consumption into Afrobarometer using a model estimated on 49 household-expenditure surveys in 25 countries, with 100 draws per respondent calibrated to the World Bank’s national distributions. Each draw is classified under five published middle-class definitions, for adults in Rounds 8 and 9 (the adult series) and for households in Rounds 3 to 9 (the household series). In hold-out tests, the share at or above the Banerjee–Duflo upper bracket has a mean absolute error of 2.3 percentage points for an excluded survey wave and 7.0 for an excluded country. That share averages 28.5 percent across adult country-rounds, and bounded middle-class shares run from 9.8 to 68.5 percent across definitions. In the household series the middle-class share is higher by a median of 25.2 points in urban than in rural households and by 23.7 points for respondents with secondary education.






Mapping Africa’s Middle Class Across Space
with Tobias Heidland
Working paper (Last updated November 2026)
Paper (SSRN) · Data (Zenodo)

We provide the first highly granular mapping of the African middle class. Using incomes from the Gallup World Poll to calculate subnational middle-class shares in 45 countries between 2015 and 2023, infrastructure, night lights, population, and gridded measures of output and wealth, we then use a machine learning approach to predict shares for 159,698 populated cells. In leave-one-country-out cross-validation, the model explains 72 percent of the regional variation in the share of people living on $2–10 a day and 62 percent for $10–100 a day. Our approach cannot predict relative definitions well. We find that 20.2 percent of Africans fall in the $2–10 band and 2.6 percent in the $10–100 band. Two-thirds of both groups live within 300 km of the coast. Both are concentrated in regions where aid disbursements are small relative to GDP.
